title: Chapter XXXVII
summary: At Ferndean, Jane finds Rochester blind, maimed, and sunk in isolation. She restores herself first through voice and touch, then explains that she is rich, has family, and is her own mistress. Her playful account of St. John revives Rochester's jealousy and makes clear that she returns from choice, not pity. Rochester proposes again, and Jane accepts without sacrifice: legal obstacle, financial dependence, and his former monopoly on power are gone. He acknowledges his wrongdoing and repentance. Their accounts show that his midnight cry and her distant answer occurred at the same moment.
events: Jane reveals herself to Rochester at Ferndean and promises that he will not remain desolate.
She tells him of her independent fortune, recovered family, and refusal of St. John.
Rochester asks Jane to marry him again, and she freely accepts.
Rochester describes his repentance and the same supernatural exchange of voices Jane experienced at Moor House.

characters.name: Jane Eyre
characters.development: Returns as a financially secure woman with alternatives, making service to Rochester an expression of desire rather than subordination.

characters.name: Edward Rochester
characters.development: Learns to receive help, confesses wrong and pride, and asks rather than engineers Jane's consent.

characters.name: St. John Rivers
characters.development: Functions in Jane's account as the loveless alternative that clarifies why Rochester suits her nature.

threads.text: Jane and Rochester reunite only after Jane has gained money, family, work, and freedom.
Rochester's call and Jane's response are confirmed as simultaneous experiences.
The renewed proposal is lawful, informed, and freely accepted.
